questions.stem: A 68-year-old man presented with urosepsis. He had a history of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Urine cultures demonstrated a sensitive Escherichia coli. CT demonstrated gas within the left kidney and retroperitoneum. He was treated with oral ciprofloxacin but clinically deteriorated on day 3 of the admission with fever, tachycardia, and hypotension.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to endocrinology for optimization of glycemic control

questions.explanation: Surgical referral for nephrectomy This question reviews the diagnosis of emphysematous pyelonephritis. Surgical management is often required, i.e., resection. Case mortality is high; diabetes mellitus and obstruction are risk factors.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q18

questions.stem: A 37-year-old, 30-week pregnant (G1P0), woman presented for routine obstetric care. She denied any urinary frequency, dysuria, or suprapubic pain. She had no known drug allergies. Urine culture was performed and demonstrated 105 colony forming units per mL Escherichia coli. A second specimen confirmed the presence of E. coli.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Cephalexin Treatment is indicated as asymptomatic bacteriuria is associated with a greater risk of subsequent pyelonephritis and consequent preterm delivery. Depending on local resistance rates, the organism may not be reliably susceptible to amoxicillin, and many labs may not test its susceptibility. Fluoroquinolones are not recommended in pregnancy. Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole would be ok earlier in pregnancy but in later pregnancy is associated with greater risk of kernicterus and hyperbilirubinemia in the newborn.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q18

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented unwell with fever, loin pain, and vomiting. He had no known allergies. On examination, his temperature was 39.4°C, his blood pressure was 98/56 mmHg, and his heart rate was 115 beats/ minute. He had right-sided renal angle tenderness. Investigations: Total white cell count 12 ×109/L Neutrophils 9 ×109/L eGFR >60 mL/min/1.73m2
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?
questions.explanation: Ciprofloxacin + stat aminoglycoside This male patient has a complicated UTI until proven otherwise thus requiring investigation for evidence of obstruction, especially if slow to resolve. He requires antibiotic selection that will provide good serum levels. You may even consider a stat dose of third-generation cephalosporin while awaiting sensitivities, but this is not given as an option. Nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin are only appropriate for lower urinary tract infection whereas this patient is systemically unwell so more likely to have upper tract infection. Grampositive cover might be required in the context of Staphylococcus aureus (hematogenous spread) pyelonephritis/renal abscess, but the stem might give additional information regarding risk factors for S. aureus bacteremia, e.g., intravenous drug use history. First-line treatment should focus on more common uropathogens: Enterobacteriaceae. This patient is systemically unwell with upper urinary tract signs and significantly abnormal labs; sexually transmitted infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae or Chlamydia trachomatis is not the likely cause.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q22

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman (14/40; G1, P0) attending for routine antenatal check had a urine culture sent. She was generally well and had not experienced any dysuria or increased urinary frequency. MSU: ≥105 cfu/mL Escherichia coli, fully sensitive. A repeat MSU was taken and the same organism was isolated again.
questions.lead_in: What is a recognized complication of this condition?
questions.explanation: Preterm delivery This patient has asymptomatic bacteriuria as evidenced by the positive urinalysis without any symptoms. Asymptomatic bacteriuria is associated with preterm delivery which is why guidelines suggest routine screening in pregnancy, with treatment and test of cure if found. Screening should be by urine culture rather than by urine dipstick as sensitivity is greater. Two consecutive specimens with the same organism are required to confirm the diagnosis. Pregnant women with asymptomatic bacteriuria also have a 20–30-fold increased risk of developing pyelonephritis and to have infants of low birthweight.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q21

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fever, fatigue, and occasional rigors. He had undergone deceased donor kidney transplantation for polycystic kidney disease 26 years ago and was on azathioprine and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. He had had recurrent episodes of fever, rigors, and sepsis for several months with blood cultures positive for Escherichia coli. Investigations: Blood cultures positive for E. coli Urinalysis: +1 protein and trace blood; urine cultures no growth An infected cyst was considered as a potential nidus of relapsing infection
questions.lead_in: What is the most sensitive diagnostic modality to detect cyst infection?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
MRI of the abdomen and pelvis

questions.explanation: Positron emission tomography scan A large retrospective study performed at a referral center in France showed that PET scan was superior to ultrasound, CT scan, and MRI for the detection of infected cysts.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q38

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presented for routine clinic review. She had insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus and was 4 years postrenal transplant. She denied urinary frequency, dysuria, or focal symptoms. Her graft function was excellent. Investigations: Urine microscopy: 30 leucocytes per high-powered field Urine culture: pure heavy growth of Candida species
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Reassurance only There is no indication to treat asymptomatic candiduria in this clinical context. Pyuria is not an indication for treatment.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q21

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented with dysuria, urinary frequency, and fevers. He had a history of spinal injury and required intermittent self-catheterization. He had previously had recurrent urinary tract infections and ciprofloxacin-associated tendinopathy. On examination he was unwell. His temperature was 38.5°C and his heart rate 120 beats/min. Rectal examination revealed a very tender prostate.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric treatment?
questions.explanation: Meropenem This man has acute prostatitis and is systemically unwell. He has a history of recurrent catheterization-associated urinary tract infection and will not tolerate FLQ. In addition, he may be at risk of a drug-resistant Pseudomonas species, and so a carbapenem is a reasonable initial regimen. Ertapenem will not cover Pseudomonas. Treatment for STI is not appropriate as first line in this clinical context. Also considering the patient’s age and background history, a focus on Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas is more appropriate.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q22

questions.question: Asymptomatic bacteriuria: indications for treatment.

parts.text: Give two indications to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

parts_raw.text: 2 indications to treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

questions.model_answer: (1) Pregnancy (screen at 12-16 weeks and treat to reduce pyelonephritis). (2) Before a traumatic genitourinary procedure associated with mucosal bleeding (e.g., transurethral prostatectomy/percutaneous lithotomy), to reduce post-procedure bacteremia/sepsis. [A third accepted indication is the early post-renal-transplantation period.]

cohort_answer.text: Pregnancy, invasive urological procedure, within 1 month post renal transplant.

For each of the following scenarios, say if you would treat or not a urine culture with > 10^8 CFU/L. 65 year old diabetic with recurrent urinary tract infections. 12 weeks pregnant patient. 83 year old lady in longterm care facility, refused to eat 2 days ago but now fine. 55 year old male about to have transurethral resection of prostate in 4 days

parts.text: For each scenario, state whether you would treat a urine culture with > 10^8 CFU/L: 65-year-old diabetic with recurrent UTIs; patient 12 weeks pregnant; 83-year-old woman in long-term care who refused to eat 2 days ago but is now well; 55-year-old man about to undergo transurethral resection of the prostate in 4 days.

parts_raw.text: For each of the following scenarios, say if you would treat or not a urine culture with > 10^8 CFU/L: 65 year old diabetic with recurrent urinary tract infections; 12 weeks pregnant patient; 83 year old lady in longterm care facility, refused to eat 2 days ago but now fine; 55 year old male about to have transurethral resection of prostate in 4 days

questions.model_answer: (1) 65 yo diabetic, recurrent UTI (asymptomatic now): Do NOT treat — no demonstrated benefit of treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in diabetics; treatment adds toxicity and may increase symptomatic infection. (2) 12 weeks pregnant: TREAT — asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated to reduce pyelonephritis (and associated preterm birth/low birth weight). (3) 83 yo LTC, now well: Do NOT treat — asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults carries no benefit from treatment; seek another cause for the transient behaviour change. (4) Pre-TURP man: TREAT — traumatic GU procedure with mucosal bleeding; eradicating bacteriuria reduces post-procedure bacteremia/sepsis.

cohort_answer.text: 65yo diabetic: No treatment (treatment has SE and is not associated with reduction in symptomatic UTI, nor alters course of diabetic nephropathy). 12wk pregnant: Treat since pregnant. 83yo LTC: No treatment. Pre-TURP: Treat (reduce risk of post operative sepsis).

questions.question: Staphylococcus saprophyticus.
questions.question_raw: 24. Staphylococcus saprophyticus:

parts.text: What microbiologic test differentiates Staphylococcus saprophyticus from Staphylococcus epidermidis?
Where does it typically cause infection, and what is the risk factor?

parts_raw.text: What microbiologic test would differentiate it from S.epidermidis?
Where does it typically cause infection? What is the risk factor?

questions.model_answer: a) Novobiocin susceptibility testing: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin-resistant, whereas S. epidermidis is novobiocin-susceptible (both are coagulase-negative). b) It typically causes uncomplicated urinary tract infection (acute cystitis); the main risk factor is recent sexual activity, and it occurs predominantly in young women.
questions.beyond_mandell: Novobiocin resistance and the S. saprophyticus cystitis association are standard microbiology (Mandell Staphylococcus chapter / Murray Medical Microbiology); not covered in the UTI chapter text read.

cohort_answer.text: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant; S. epidermidis is novobiocin sensitive. Typically causes UTI; risk factor is sexual activity, more common in females than males

questions.question: A hospitalized woman with an indwelling Foley catheter, post-appendectomy, has cloudy foul-smelling urine, temperature 37.2°C, WBC 12, and is otherwise asymptomatic. Urine culture grows a susceptible organism and urinalysis shows some leukocytes. What would you do?
questions.question_raw: A woman in hospital with cloudy foul smelling urine with indwelling foley. T 37.2C, WBC 12, post-op appendectomy. Otherwise no symptoms. Growing something that's pretty sensitive in Ucx, some leuks on UA.

parts.text: What would you do?

parts_raw.text: What would you do?

questions.model_answer: This is catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria: she is afebrile with no urinary symptoms, and cloudy/foul urine and pyuria are nonspecific in a catheterized patient. (1) Do NOT prescribe antibiotics — screening for and treating ASB in short-term (<30 day) catheterized patients is not recommended and only selects for resistance. (2) Remove the Foley if it is no longer required (short-term post-op catheter). (3) Monitor clinically and treat only if true CAUTI signs/symptoms not explained by another cause emerge.

cohort_answer.text: Remove Foley. No abx indicated. IDSA: in patients with short-term indwelling urethral catheter (<30 days), recommend against screening for or treating asymptomatic bacteriuria (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence)

questions.model_answer:
a) RR = (30/200) ÷ (10/200) = 0.15 ÷ 0.05 = 3. The risk of death is 3-fold higher in UTI patients than matched controls.
b) (1) Infectious diseases physician (accountable program leader); (2) clinical pharmacist with infectious diseases expertise (co-leader).

questions.model_answer: a) The two most common carbapenemases are KPC (most common in North America) and NDM (OXA-48-like is the next most common metallo-/serine enzyme). b) For an NDM (metallo-beta-lactamase) producer: (1) Cefiderocol; (2) Ceftazidime-avibactam PLUS aztreonam (the combination restores activity against metallo-beta-lactamases). These are the preferred options since NDM hydrolyzes carbapenems and is not inhibited by avibactam/vaborbactam/relebactam alone.

2 most common carbapenemases: KPC (most common in North America), NDM, OXA-48-like (PHAC data: KPC 48.7%, NDM 28.2%, OXA-48 14.8%).
2 first line treatment options for cystitis caused by CRE: Nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin are preferred (though likelihood of susceptibility is low); alternatives include single dose aminoglycoside, oral fosfomycin (E. coli only), colistin, ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, cefiderocol. For pyelonephritis/cUTI: TMP-SMX, ciprofloxacin, or levofloxacin preferred if susceptibility demonstrated; ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-cilastatin-relebactam, and cefiderocol also preferred; aminoglycosides are alternatives.

questions.model_answer: a) 7 days (fluoroquinolone; ceftriaxone/oral beta-lactam course 10-14 days, but shortest evidence-based fluoroquinolone course is 7 days). b) 7 days: source-controlled uncomplicated gram-negative bacteremia is non-inferior at 7 vs 14 days (Yahav/von Dach trials). c) 6 months: 2 months RIPE intensive phase then 4 months rifampin/isoniazid continuation. d) 14 days from the first negative blood culture: uncomplicated catheter-associated SAB qualifies for a 14-day course when the focus is removed, endocarditis is excluded, follow-up cultures are negative, fever resolves by 72 h, and no metastatic foci are present. e) 5 days: minimum for CAP if clinically stable and afebrile 48-72 h. f) 4 days after adequate source control (STOP-IT trial).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the S. aureus bacteremia duration is from this chapter (p. 2426); the pyelonephritis (7 d FQ), gram-negative bacteremia (7 d, Yahav 2019/von Dach 2020), TB (6 mo, ATS/CDC/PHAC), CAP (5 d, ATS/IDSA), and diverticulitis (4 d post-source-control, STOP-IT/Sawyer 2015) durations rest on those trials/guidelines, not on Mandell ch. 194.

parts.text: Would you treat?
If so, with what?
What simple laboratory test distinguishes C. albicans from non-albicans?

parts_raw.text: Would you treat
If so, with what?
What simple laboratory test distinguishes C. albicans from non-albicans?

questions.model_answer:
a) No. Asymptomatic candiduria usually resolves without antifungal therapy and treatment is not indicated. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic patients or those at high risk for dissemination: neutropenic patients, very-low-birth-weight infants, renal transplant recipients, and patients undergoing urologic instrumentation or with urinary tract obstruction. A stone without obstruction and no dissemination risk does not warrant treatment; treat instead if he is symptomatic or about to undergo an instrumentation/urologic procedure.
b) If treatment is indicated (e.g., symptomatic cystitis or planned instrumentation), oral fluconazole 200 mg (3 mg/kg) daily for ~2 weeks for a susceptible isolate; alternatives are AMB-D 0.3-0.6 mg/kg for 1-7 days or flucytosine. Relief of any obstruction and removal of stents/catheters is the primary step. Fungus balls require surgical removal.
c) The germ tube test.

cohort_answer.text: No treatment for asymptomatic candiduria unless high risk for dissemination (neutropenic patients, very low-birth-weight infants <1500g, patients undergoing urologic manipulation); renal transplantation no longer an absolute indication, consider case-by-case (UpToDate). Treatment: not recommended unless high-risk group; neutropenic/VLBW infants treated as for candidemia; patients undergoing urologic procedures: oral fluconazole 400mg (6mg/kg) daily OR AmB deoxycholate 0.3-0.6mg/kg daily for several days before/after procedure; for symptomatic cystitis: oral fluconazole 200mg (3mg/kg) daily x2 weeks, alternatively 1-7 days amphoB deoxycholate or flucytosine x7-10 days; if treating pyelo with amphoB can add flucytosine; do not use lipid formulations of amphoB (does not concentrate in kidney/bladder). Distinguishing test: Germ tube testing.
